data.title: Insufficient Network Segmentation
data.summary:
The internal network permitted unrestricted communication between systems of
differing security requirements, allowing compromise of a single low-value host
to reach critical infrastructure without obstruction.
data.description:
Systems of materially different sensitivity were found to share unrestricted
network reachability. Workstations could reach domain controllers, database
servers, and management interfaces directly on their administrative ports, and no
filtering was observed between the segments concerned.

Network segmentation exists to ensure that compromise of one system does not
translate into access to the entire estate. Where it is absent, an attacker who
gains a foothold anywhere obtains the same network position as if they had
compromised the most sensitive system in the environment, and can enumerate and
attack every host without needing to defeat any further control.

The absence of segmentation also removes an opportunity for detection. Traffic
crossing a boundary can be inspected and alerted upon; traffic within a flat
network is typically neither logged nor examined, so lateral movement produces no
signal.

This condition amplifies every other weakness present. A vulnerability confined
to one segment represents a contained risk; the same vulnerability on a flat
network represents a route to complete compromise.
data.impact:
Compromise of any single host, including a low-value workstation reached through
phishing, would provide an attacker with unrestricted network access to critical
infrastructure including domain controllers and database systems. This removes
any requirement for the attacker to defeat further network controls, and
substantially reduces the likelihood that lateral movement is detected before the
environment is fully compromised.
data.recommendation:
1. Define network zones based on the sensitivity and function of the systems they
   contain, separating user workstations, general servers, critical
   infrastructure, and management interfaces.

2. Implement filtering between zones permitting only the specific traffic
   required by business function, denying all other traffic by default.

3. Place all administrative interfaces on a dedicated management network
   reachable only from authorised administrative systems, so that a compromised
   workstation cannot reach them.

4. Restrict communication between workstations, as direct workstation-to-workstation
   traffic is rarely required and is a primary mechanism of lateral movement.

5. Log and monitor traffic crossing zone boundaries, so that lateral movement
   attempts generate a signal that can be investigated.

6. Validate the effectiveness of segmentation through periodic testing, as rules
   added over time to resolve operational problems frequently erode the intended
   boundaries.
